setup.zh: 舅舅送你走了三天；前一夜，你把最后半张饼分给了牛棚里的孙二狗。天没亮，码头上一个穿白的人拿一块石头，买走了一个五六岁的孩子。三百级石阶直通云雾，顶上站着一个扫地的老头：「不看出身，不看荐书——只看三样：腿，脑子，胆子。」一试，腿：三百级，一炷香。
setup.en: Your uncle walked you three days; the night before, you gave the last half flatbread to Sun Ergou in the cowshed. Before dawn, on the riverbank, a man in white bought a child of five or six with a stone and an ingot. Three hundred stone steps climb into the clouds, and at the top stands an old sweeper: "Not by birth, not by letters of recommendation — by three things only: legs, head, nerve." First trial, legs: three hundred steps, one stick of incense.

recap.zh: 一试，三百级石阶：你三步一吸，三步一呼，替舅舅走了上来。
recap.en: First trial, three hundred steps: three steps a breath in, three a breath out, you climbed the stair for your uncle.

zh: 石阶顶上，一个扫地的老头。
en: Three hundred steps, straight into the clouds.
At the top, an old man with a broom.
First trial, legs: one stick of incense.

story.zh:
九月初七晌午，沈小满跟着舅舅，走在往泗水去的大路上，身后一阵吆喝，一顶滑竿从人堆当中颠了过去，滑竿上坐着马小宝，手里一块桂花糕。马三跟在边上，胸口鼓鼓的，揣着一封荐书。

马家那封荐书，小满倒不怎么怕；他心里最怕的，是一块石头。舅舅说，三试都过了，还要进正殿，把手按在一块测灵石上，那石头照着人身上的灵气亮，亮什么颜色，便是什么灵根。胸口木牌里的银月，临睡前只留给他一个字：「藏。」那石头要是一亮，亮出一道银光、亮出一条狐狸尾巴来，满殿的人都瞧见了——他不敢往下想。他问过木牌三回，木牌凉凉的，一回也没答。

越往南，路上往泗水去的人越多，到后来一眼望不到头，几千户人家，赶的是同一个日子。

九月初八傍晚，到了泗水边上。

小满先是闻见的。风从山上下来，一口吸进去，凉丝丝、甜丝丝的，像三伏天喝了一口刚打上来的井水，一直凉到肚脐眼底下。他还没抬头，脚先停了。

沉鼎山并不怎么高，只是陡。山脚下的松林里浮着一层极淡的白气，在树梢中间慢慢地游；山腰以上，云雾缠得严严实实，一道石阶从山脚笔直地插进雾里去，瞧不见尽头。石阶顶上，就是沉鼎观的山门。小满张着嘴，胸口那块木牌，轻轻地烫了一下。

山脚下的客栈早住满了，最好的一间上房，叫蒙山马家包了去。庙里的廊檐底下也躺满了人。廊柱边上生着一堆火，火边坐着一个汉子，一脸横肉，腰里别一把短刀，刀鞘上缠着红绸。他姓葛，行六，是马家雇来护送少爷的镖师；马家没给他留铺，他便在廊下喝马家的酒。

几个孩子围着火烤手，问他是不是也来考的。葛六道：「考过了。二十年前。外门，练气三层。」他从怀里摸出一颗核桃，两根指头一捏，「咔」的一声，碎了。「三层，就这点本事。练气统共九层，九层上头还有一道门槛，叫筑基——跨过去，才算进了仙门的屋。我在第三层蹲了六年，下山走镖。」

一个当爹的问：「那筑基……难么？」葛六伸出一根指头，在火边一圈孩子的脸上点过去：「你们这几千个，明天爬上去、测完了、进了门的，一百来个。一百来个里头，将来能筑基的——一个。」

廊下静了，火里一根柴「噼」地爆了一下。小满憋不住，问道：「大叔，百日筑基——是不是一百天？」葛六笑了：「百日，是打底子。我打了六年。」小满在心里把那富余的八十三天，一笔划掉了。

一个光脚的孩子忽然站起来，大声道：「那我就当那一个！」满廊的人都笑了。那孩子不笑，道：「我家七张嘴，二亩坡地。今年的豆子，收上来的比种下去的还少。」他把下巴一抬，「一年五两。够他们吃三年。」廊下又静了。葛六没笑，道：「……我当年，也这么说。」

这时候一个马家的家丁挑着灯笼找了过来，压低了嗓子道：「葛镖头，三爷问，你说的那个摆法，画好了没有？」葛六拍了拍胸口：「画好了。五两银子，一个格子也不差。」跟着灯笼走了。小满只记住了「五两银子」和「格子」。

舅舅花了十个铜钱，在一户人家的牛棚里赁到半张草铺。草铺那头睡着一个瘦孩子，十四五岁，瘦得像一根晾衣竿，背着一个比他身子还大的包袱，一声不吭。

那天夜里，小满摸出了最后那张饼，掰下一半塞进嘴里，一抬头，那瘦孩子还醒着，正盯着他手里剩的那半张，喉头一动一动的。

小满想起谷底那一夜，他掰给那只断了尾巴的小狐狸的那一半饼，便把手里这半张递了过去：「吃吧。明天要爬三百级呢。」那孩子一口塞进嘴里，嚼完了，才想起来说：「……谢谢。我叫孙二狗。」小满道：「沈小满。」孙二狗道：「我记着了。」

小满肚子里只剩半张饼，心里只有一块石头。

九月初九，是重阳。天还没亮透，泗水边的码头上已经站满了人，雾贴着水面走，人的脸一张一张都是灰的。一夜里一船一船的人从下游上来，都在这儿下船；顺着河岸往上走一里来地，石阶底下拿绳子圈起来的那一片，才是沉鼎观的地。

码头上让出了一块空地。空地边上一块拴船的青石，石上站着一个人，一身白袍，白得在这一码头的泥脚印里不沾一点泥。他手里托着一块灰石头，鸡蛋大小，跟前排着一溜小孩子，大的七八岁，小的还要人抱着，都是爹娘一早领来的。他把那块石头往孩子的手心里一按，按一下，看一眼，摇摇头，下一个。他从头到尾，一声不出。

排到一个石匠模样的汉子，领着两个儿子。大的那个十二三岁，又黑又壮，一双手跟他爹一样，指节上全是老茧，石头按上去，还是一块灰石头，什么也没亮。白衣人摇了摇头。小的那个五六岁，还拖着鼻涕，石头一按上去，忽地亮了——亮成一片青，青得像开春头一茬麦苗，一种颜色，干干净净，一点杂色也没有。

白衣人这才点了点头，从袖子里摸出一锭银子，放进那汉子的手心里，把他的手指头一根一根合上。小满离得近，看见了那锭银子翻过来的底：錾着一个记号，一个圈，圈里一横。

他身上一凉。那记号他没见过，却听人说过：冬月里井台边那个货郎，说岷江那边有个穿白的，拿一包银子换走了一个才落地七天的娃，那银子的锭底，就錾着一个圈，圈里一横。

这一身白，小满背上的汗毛先立了起来。他往人堆后头缩了半步，缩到一个挑担子的汉子身后，再看时，那人的脸隔着雾，瞧不真；嗓子，他一声也没出。穿白的，天底下不止一个。胸口的木牌冰凉，一动不动。他还是想起爹在柴垛顶上说的那一句：它听见的不是你喘，是你心慌。他便把一口气吐得又细又长，吐到底，再慢慢吸回来。那白衣人从头到尾，没往这边看一眼。

那汉子捧着银子，跪下去，给白衣人磕了一个头；又转过身，给他那个小儿子磕了一个头。小孩子不懂，看着他爹的后脑勺，咯咯地笑。白衣人把他抱起来，往河岸上走，岸上停着一辆青篷马车。走到半路，那孩子才觉出不对来，在白衣人怀里扭着身子，伸着两只手，哇地哭了：「哥——」

那个大的追了两步，给他爹一把揪住了领子。马车走了。岸边站着一个五十上下的人，灰袍，生着一张没睡醒的脸，白衣人上车之前，冲他点了一点头，他也点了一点头，转身往石阶那边去了。

人堆里有人小声道：「太华山上的太一宫来的。隔几年来一回，专挑一种颜色的娃娃。」又有人道：「他不上山。山门底下是沉鼎观的地，码头不是。赶在开山门前头，先挑一遍。」又有人道：「一锭，十两。」

石匠把那锭银子揣进怀里，揣得很深，回头对大儿子道：「你也上去。考上了，一年五两；考不上，别回来。家里还有三张嘴。」说完，他往北走了，一次也没有回头。

那大孩子站在码头上，没有哭。他转过脸来，看见小满正看着他，便道：「那石头……亮了，就是仙人要的？」小满道：「……嗯。」那孩子道：「他们把小豆带哪儿去了？」小满答不上来。那孩子低头看了看自己的手，那一双手刚才按在石头上，石头没亮。他道：「我要是也亮了，他们就把我也带去了。」

小满问他叫什么。他道：「石蛋。」

石阶底下，拿绳子圈了一片空地，十几个穿灰袍的执事站在里头，查验年纪（十二起）、籍贯，一人发一块竹牌，叫作考牌，拿烧红的铁签子当场烙上名字。唱名的那个执事，五十上下，生着一张没睡醒的脸，一面唱名，一面打呵欠——小满认得这张脸：天不亮的时候，码头上，白衣人上马车之前冲他点过一点头的，就是他。他拿竹牌敲着手心道：「三试，一试画一道。三道画满，进正殿测灵；牌子丢了，便算你没来过。有荐书的，哪一试没过，许补——怎么补，执事说了算。」刀剑弓棍一律解下来，挂在一面木架上，拿竹签子记了名字，说是傍晚抬上山门，入了门的自己去领。小满把爷爷那张弓挂了上去，缠满牛筋的弓背夹在一排亮闪闪的刀剑中间，活像一条打了补丁的裤子混在一群新衣裳里。小满记住了那弓挂在第三排左数第七个，把考牌揣进怀里，贴着那块木牌。

便在这时，人群后头一阵骚动：「让一让！马家少爷来了！」马家的滑竿到了，一个家丁给马小宝打伞，一个给他扇扇子——这一天既没下雨，也没出太阳。马三跟在滑竿边上，时不时隔着衣裳按一按怀里那封信，像按着一只会飞的鸟。滑竿后头，走着葛六。马小宝一眼瞧见了小满，下巴一扬，拿两个鼻孔对着他：「哟，沈小满，你们家那扇门，扛回来没有？」小满道：「扛回来了，小宝哥。装得有点歪。」

辰时差一刻，泗水忽然静了。

不是风停，是水停。宽宽的一条河，正往东淌着，忽然像给谁按住了，一个浪头也不起，平得像一面磨过的铜镜。河边几千口人，说话的不说了，哭的也不哭了，谁也没叫谁，一齐往河里望。河心里，水往两边分开，分出一道沟来，沟底慢慢浮起一样东西——起先当是一块礁石，青黑色，长满了水苔，浮出来，才看出是一面背壳，比河边泊着的渡船还大，壳上的纹路一格一格，像一块田。那是一只鼋。它把一颗比磨盘还大的脑袋探出水面，眯着两只老眼，慢慢地往岸边游，游过的地方，水在它身后合拢，不起一个浪花。鼋背上站着一个人，一身灰袍，两只手拢在袖子里。鼋游过码头，那人的眼睛往码头上那块空地一落——青篷马车的车辙还新着——脸色登时沉了下来，两道眉毛竖了起来，低声道：「大胆狂徒，胆敢在我沉鼎观门口抢人。日后，定要登门讨个说法。」

小满只觉得胸口一沉，像有人在他背上压了一扇门板，压得他膝盖一软——他身前身后的人，已经一个接一个跪了下去，没有一个人叫他们跪。小满也跪下了，跪下了才知道，那不是他自己要跪的，是那一股看不见的分量，从河上压过来，压得满河边的人都直不起腰。鼋到了岸边，那人从鼋背上一步跨到石阶底下，又一步，已到了半山腰，再一步，便没进了云里。那只鼋把脑袋缩回去，沉进了泗水，水面上一个漩儿也没留下。河又淌起来了，压在背上的那扇门板，跟着没了。人们一个一个爬起来，拍膝盖上的泥，谁也不说话。半天，才有个老汉小声道：「……观主。沉鼎观的观主。」

辰时正，山门上「当」的一声钟，几千个孩子霎时间静了下来。石阶顶上，不知什么时候站了一个扫地的老头，一身灰布短褂，拄着一把竹扫帚，佝偻着背，看都不看底下一眼，只顾一下一下地扫他脚底下那一级台阶——第三百级，最上头那一级。这三百级石阶，连上头山门前那片石坪，天没亮他便从底下扫起，一级一级扫上来，扫到这一级，便站住了，扫得最久。观里的老弟子说，这老头扫这三百级扫了五十年。扫了好一会儿，他才开口，声音不高，一个字一个字清清楚楚地落到山脚下来：「沉鼎观收人。不看出身，不看荐书——」人群里「嗡」的一声。马三的那只手，僵在了胸口上。那老头接着道：「——只看三样。腿。脑子。胆子。」说完，他又低头扫地。

石阶顶上，一个执事点着了一炷香，插在一只铜炉里，喊了一声：「开始！」

一试考腿：三百级石阶，一级齐膝高，一炷香。「开始」两个字还没落地，几千个孩子便一窝蜂地往上冲，你推我搡，喊爹的、喊娘的、踩了别人鞋的、给别人踩了鞋的，草鞋布鞋掉了一路，有一个一跟头栽在台阶上，爬起来光着一只脚接着冲，乱成一锅粥，活像一群给人打开了笼门的鸭子。绳子外头，爹娘们喊名字的声音一浪高过一浪：「二牛——慢点——」「宝儿，别回头——」「三步一口气——」这最后一句，是舅舅喊的。
story.en:
Noon on the seventh of the ninth month: Shen Xiaoman and his uncle were on the high road to the Si. A shout from behind, and a sedan chair came jolting straight through the crowd, Ma Xiaobao in it, an osmanthus cake in hand. Ma San walked beside it, his chest bulging with a letter of recommendation.

The Ma family's letter didn't frighten Xiaoman much. What he feared most was a stone. His uncle said that once the three trials were passed you went into the main hall and put your hand on a spirit-testing stone, and the stone lit by the spirit in you: whatever colours it showed, that was your root. Yinyue, asleep in the token on his chest, had left him one word before she slept: "Hide." If that stone lit up and showed a streak of silver, a fox's tail, with the whole hall watching — he didn't dare think further. He had asked the token three times. It stayed cool, and never answered once.

The farther south, the more people on the road bound for the Si, until there was no end to them — several thousand households, racing the same day.

At dusk on the eighth they reached the Si.

Xiaoman smelled it first. The wind came down off the mountain, and one breath went in cool and sweet, like a mouthful of water fresh from the well in the dog days, cool all the way down below his navel. Before he even looked up, his feet had stopped.

Mount Chending wasn't very high, only steep. In the pine wood at its foot floated a very faint white breath, drifting slowly among the treetops; from the waist up the mountain was wound tight in cloud, and a stone stair ran straight from its foot into the mist, no end in sight. At the top of the stair stood the gate of Chending Temple. Xiaoman stood with his mouth open, and the wooden token on his chest grew faintly warm.

The inns at the foot of the mountain were long since full — the best upstairs room taken by the Ma family of Mount Meng — and the temple veranda was full of people lying down too. By a pillar burned a fire, and beside it sat a heavy-jowled man, a short knife at his belt, its sheath wound in red silk. His name was Ge, sixth son — the escort the Mas had hired to see the young master there; the Mas had left him no bed, so he drank the Mas' wine under the veranda.

A few children warming their hands at the fire asked him whether he'd come to sit the trials too. Ge Liu said, "Sat them already. Twenty years ago. Outer court, third level of qi refining." He took a walnut from his coat and pinched it between two fingers — *crack* — and it broke. "Third level, and that's all it's good for. Qi refining has nine levels, and above the ninth there's one more threshold, called foundation building — step over it and you're inside the immortal house. I squatted on the third for six years, then came down the mountain to guard caravans."

A father asked, "And this foundation building… is it hard?" Ge Liu held up one finger and pointed it round the ring of children's faces by the fire. "You few thousand — the ones who climb up tomorrow, get tested and get through the gate: a hundred or so. Out of that hundred or so, the ones who'll ever build a foundation — one."

The veranda went quiet; a stick in the fire popped. Xiaoman couldn't hold it in. "Uncle — a hundred days to build a foundation — is that really a hundred days?" Ge Liu laughed. "A hundred days is laying the groundwork. I laid mine for six years." In his head Xiaoman crossed out the eighty-three spare days with one stroke.

A barefoot boy suddenly stood up and said loudly, "Then I'll be that one!" The whole veranda laughed. The boy didn't. "Seven mouths at home, two mu of hillside. This year we harvested fewer beans than we sowed." He lifted his chin. "Five taels a year. That feeds them three years." The veranda went quiet again. Ge Liu didn't laugh. "…I said that too, once."

Just then a Ma servant came looking with a lantern, and said low: "Escort Ge, Third Master asks — that layout you told him of, have you drawn it?" Ge Liu patted his chest. "Drawn. Five taels, not one square off." He followed the lantern away. Xiaoman only remembered "five taels" and "squares".

For ten coppers his uncle rented half a straw bed in someone's cowshed. At the far end of the straw slept a thin boy of fourteen or fifteen, thin as a laundry pole, with a bundle bigger than himself, and not a word out of him.

That night Xiaoman took out the last flatbread, broke off half and put it in his mouth, and looked up: the thin boy was still awake, staring at the half left in his hand, his throat working.

Xiaoman remembered that night at the bottom of the valley, and the half flatbread he had broken off for the little fox with its broken tails, and held out this half. "Eat. We've three hundred steps to climb tomorrow." The boy stuffed it in whole, and only when he'd swallowed remembered to say: "…Thank you. I'm Sun Ergou." Xiaoman said, "Shen Xiaoman." Sun Ergou said, "I'll remember."

Xiaoman had only half a flatbread in his belly, and a stone on his mind.

The ninth of the ninth month was the Double Ninth. It wasn't yet properly light, and the landing on the Si were already packed with people; the mist walked along the water, and every face was grey. All night, boat after boat had come up from downstream and put people off here; a li or so further up the bank, the roped-off ground at the foot of the steps — that was where Chending's ground began.

On the landing a space had been cleared. At its edge was a mooring stone, and on the stone stood a man in a white robe, so white that among all the muddy footprints on that landing not a speck clung to it. On his palm he held a grey stone the size of a hen's egg, and before him stood a line of small children, the eldest seven or eight, the youngest still carried, each brought down early by a father or mother. He pressed the stone into each child's palm — a press, a look, a shake of the head, next. From first to last he made no sound.

Then came a man who looked like a stonemason, with two sons. The elder was twelve or thirteen, dark and sturdy, his hands like his father's, calloused at every knuckle; the stone pressed into them stayed dusty grey and lit nothing. The man in white shook his head. The younger was five or six, his nose still running; the moment the stone touched him it lit — lit a sheet of green, green as the first wheat shoots of spring, a single colour, clean, without a fleck of anything else.

Only then did the man in white nod. He took a silver ingot from his sleeve, set it in the mason's palm, and folded the man's fingers over it one by one. Xiaoman was close enough to see the underside as it turned: a mark struck into it — a circle, with a bar across the middle.

He went cold. He had never seen that mark, but he had heard of it: that winter the pedlar by the well had told of a man in white on the Min River who traded a bundle of silver for a baby seven days old — and struck into the base of that silver was a circle, with a bar across it.

That white — the hair on Xiaoman's back stood up before he knew why. He shrank half a step back into the crowd, behind a man with a carrying pole, and looked again: through the mist the face wouldn't come clear, and the voice — the man hadn't made a sound. There was more than one man in white under heaven. The token on his chest was icy and did not stir. Still he remembered what his father had said on top of the woodpile: it doesn't hear you panting, it hears your heart racing. So he let a breath out thin and long, all the way, and slowly drew it back in. From first to last the man in white never looked his way.

The mason, holding the silver, knelt and knocked his head once to the man in white; then he turned and knocked his head once to his little son. The little boy didn't understand; he looked at the back of his father's head and giggled. The man in white picked him up and walked toward the bank, where a covered cart with a blue awning stood waiting. Halfway there the child sensed something wrong, twisted in the man's arms, reached out both hands, and burst into tears: "Brother —"

The elder boy ran two steps and was caught by the collar by his father. The cart left. On the bank stood a man of fifty or so in a grey robe, with a face that looked as if it had never quite woken up; before the man in white climbed in, he gave the grey robe a nod, and the grey robe nodded back and turned away toward the stair.

Someone in the crowd said under his breath: "From the Taiyi Palace, up on Mount Taihua. Comes every few years, and picks out only the one-colour babies." Someone else said: "He doesn't go up the mountain. Under the gate is Chending's ground; the landing isn't. He gets his pick before the gate opens." Someone else said, "One ingot — ten taels."

The mason tucked the ingot into his coat, deep, and turned to his elder son. "You go up too. Get in, it's five taels a year; don't get in, don't come back. There are three more mouths at home." With that he walked off north, and not once did he look back.

The elder boy stood on the landing and didn't cry. He turned his face, saw Xiaoman looking at him, and said, "That stone… if it lights, that's what the immortals want?" Xiaoman said, "…Yes." The boy said, "Where are they taking Little Dou?" Xiaoman couldn't answer. The boy looked down at his own hands — they had been pressed to the stone just now, and it hadn't lit. He said, "If mine had lit, they'd have taken me too."

Xiaoman asked his name. He said, "Shidan."

At the foot of the stair a space was roped off, and a dozen stewards in grey robes stood inside checking age (twelve and up) and home county, handing each child a bamboo slip called a trial tag and burning the name into it on the spot with a red-hot iron spike. The steward calling the names, fifty or so, with a face that looked as if it had never quite woken up, yawned between names — Xiaoman knew that face: before dawn, on the landing, the man in white had nodded to him before climbing into the cart. He tapped a slip on his palm. "Three trials, one stroke for each. Three strokes full, and you go into the main hall to be tested; lose your tag, and you were never here. Those with a letter of recommendation who fail a trial may make it up — how to make it up, the steward decides." Swords, knives, bows and staves all had to come off and hang on a wooden rack, tagged with a bamboo name slip; they'd be carried up to the gate at dusk, and those who got in could fetch their own. Xiaoman hung his grandfather's bow on it — the ox-sinew-wrapped back squeezed between a row of shining blades like a pair of patched trousers among new clothes. Xiaoman marked that it hung third row, seventh from the left, tucked his tag inside his coat against the wooden token.

Just then there was a stir at the back of the crowd: "Make way! Make way! The young Ma master's here!" The Ma sedan chair had arrived, one servant holding a parasol over Ma Xiaobao, another fanning him — on a day with neither rain nor sun. Ma San walked beside the chair, now and then pressing the letter in his coat through the cloth, as if pressing down a bird that might fly. Behind the chair walked Ge Liu. Ma Xiaobao spotted Xiaoman, tipped his chin up, and looked at him down both nostrils. "Well, Shen Xiaoman — that door of yours, did you carry it home?" Xiaoman said, "We did, Xiaobao-ge. Put it back a bit crooked."

A quarter before the hour of the dragon, the Si suddenly went still.

Not the wind dropping — the water stopping. The broad river had been running east, and all at once it was as if someone had pressed it flat: not one wave rose, smooth as a polished bronze mirror. Thousands of people on the bank, the talkers stopped talking, the criers stopped crying; no one told anyone, and all of them looked out at the river together. In midstream the water parted to either side, opening a trench, and up from its bottom slowly rose something — at first they took it for a reef, blue-black, thick with weed; as it surfaced they saw it was a shell, bigger than the ferry moored at the bank, its markings square on square like a field. It was a yuan, a giant softshell turtle. It pushed a head bigger than a millstone out of the water, narrowed two old eyes, and swam slowly toward the bank; where it passed, the water closed behind it without a ripple. On its back stood a man in a grey robe, hands folded in his sleeves. As the turtle passed the landing, the man's eyes fell on that empty patch of it — the wheel ruts of the blue-canopied cart still fresh — and his face darkened at once, his brows rose straight up, and he said low: "Insolent wretches — to snatch people at the very gate of my Chending Temple. One day I will go to their door and have an answer."

Xiaoman felt his chest grow heavy, as if someone had laid a door across his back, and his knees gave — before him and behind him people were going down on their knees one after another, and no one had told them to. Xiaoman knelt too, and only once he was down did he know it wasn't his own doing: an unseen weight was pressing in off the river, bending the whole bank so no one could stand straight. The turtle reached the shore; the man stepped from its back to the foot of the stair, another step and he was halfway up the mountain, one more and he was gone into the cloud. The turtle drew in its head and sank into the Si without leaving so much as an eddy. The river ran again, and the door on their backs was gone with it. People got up one by one and brushed the mud off their knees, and nobody spoke. At last an old man said quietly: "…The abbot. The abbot of Chending Temple."

At the hour of the dragon a bell struck over the gate — *dang* — and several thousand children fell silent at once. At the top of the stair, no one knew since when, stood an old man with a broom: a grey cloth jacket, a bamboo broom to lean on, a bent back; he didn't look down once, only swept the step under his feet, stroke after stroke — the three hundredth, the topmost. The whole stair of three hundred, and the stone terrace before the gate above it, he swept every day from the bottom up, starting before dawn; this step he swept last and longest, and here he stood. The temple's old disciples said he had swept those three hundred steps for fifty years. After a good while he spoke, not loudly, each word falling clear to the foot of the mountain: "Chending Temple takes disciples. Not by birth, not by letters of recommendation —" The crowd hummed. Ma San's hand froze on his chest. The old man went on: "— by three things only. Legs. Head. Nerve." That said, he bent to his sweeping again.

At the top of the stair a steward lit a stick of incense, set it in a bronze burner, and called out: "Begin!"

The first trial tested legs: three hundred stone steps, each knee-high, one stick of incense. Before "Begin" had even landed, several thousand children surged up in a mob, pushing and shoving, shouting for dads and mums, treading on shoes and trodden on, straw sandals and cloth shoes strewn all the way up, one boy pitching flat on the steps and scrambling up to charge on with one bare foot, a pot of porridge, like ducks when someone opens the cage. Outside the rope, the parents' shouting rose wave on wave: "Erniu — slow down —" "Bao'er, don't look back —" "Three steps a breath —" That last was his uncle.

label.en: At the back: three steps in, three steps out

exits.means: climbs steadily at an even pace, counting breaths, like a hunter on a long trail

story.zh:
沈小满却没有冲。他走在最后面。他爹教过他：追兔子比快，追鹿比稳；上山的路，是山的，你跟山抢，山不让你。他冲由他冲，石阶三百级；他快由他快，香只一炷香——小满心里把这两句颠来倒去地念，一级一级地走，三步一吸，三步一呼，只看脚底下这一级。

冲在最前头的那些孩子，到了一百级上下，一个一个便像腿上绑了石头：有的坐在台阶上喘，喘得张着嘴直不起腰；有的扶着崖壁，一步一挪。马小宝是两个家丁一左一右架上来的，两只脚离地半尺，在半空里一荡一荡，嘴里还嚼着桂花糕；那扫地老头在石阶顶上远远看了一眼，家丁便松了手，他「扑通」一声，一屁股坐在了一百二十级上，瘫得像一摊和稀了的泥。小满从他身边走过去，没有停。

走到一百三十级上下，他看见了一个兖州来的孩子。那孩子是跟着头一拨冲上去的，这时候扶着崖壁，脸白得像一张纸，两条腿抖得像筛糠。他看见小满，眼睛一亮，如同看见了一根救命的绳子，喊道：「兄弟！拉我一把！」

小满是想拉的。可他知道，这一拉，他三步一吸、三步一呼的那口气就断了；气一断，他自己也要在这里坐下。他爹说过，山里遇见别人掉进坑里，先看看自己脚底下站稳了没有；自己都没站稳，伸手去拉，是两个人一起掉进去。小满便没有伸手，只道：「别冲了。三步一口气。跟着我的脚。」那孩子跟着他走了十来级，到了一百四十级，终于还是一屁股坐了下去，摆着手道：「兄弟，你走，你走……」小满回头看了他一眼，走了。走出去十几级，他听见身后那孩子在哭，哭得很小声，怕人听见似的。他没有回头，心里却想：等我哪一天站得够稳了，我要拉。拉得动几个，拉几个。这念头一闪就过去了，他那时候并没有当真。

走到一百五十级，一个扎两根小辫子的姑娘从他身边冲了过去。她没坐下，也没哭，他只看见一个鼻头冻得通红的侧脸，咬着牙，一口气往上冲，冲得小辫子一甩一甩的。小满心里一跳：阿禾？临走前些日子，她在井台边上拦住他，问泗水几天的路、一天吃几张饼，记在一个他从没见过的本子上——他还当她是替她爹问的。他喊了一声：「阿禾！」那姑娘没回头，一口气冲进雾里去了。往上又走了几级，一个黑壮的身影也从他边上闷着头擦过去，指节上全是老茧，是石蛋。他不喘，也不看人，一步一步踩得极重，恨不得把石阶踩进山里去。

一百六十级到了。这一级台阶，同别的台阶没什么两样，只是边上的崖壁上，不知什么年月，给人用石头、用刀、用指甲，刻满了密密麻麻的字，一层压着一层，有的是名字，有的是年月，有的只是一道杠——都是在这一级上坐下过的人刻的。小满跨过去的时候，扭过头朝那些刻痕里多看了一眼。他不知道自己在找什么。他没有找到。

过了一百六十级，石阶便陡了，一级比一级高出半指，攒到两百级上下，攒成了一道梯子；两边的崖壁也挨近了，窄处只容两个人侧着身子过。他不往上看，也不往下看，只数：一吸，二吸，三吸；抬脚，落脚，再抬脚。雾里远远传来一下一下的沙沙声，是扫帚扫在青石上的声音，他走一级，它便近一分。

走到两百六十级上下，身后忽然一阵吆喝：「让开！让开！」是那顶滑竿，又上来了。原来马三在石阶底下，把那封信亮了出来。执事看了一眼落款，道：「荐书。许补。」四个轿夫便抬着马小宝，一路颠上来。滑竿挤过小满身边，把他挤在崖壁上，蹭破了一块皮。挤过去了，却在前头最窄的那一段停住了。马小宝在滑竿上回过头来，冲他咧嘴一笑：「慢点抬。本少爷看看风景。」

雾里什么风景也没有。四个轿夫横在石阶上，前后堵得严严实实，一只猫也钻不过去。小满抬头看——看不见铜炉，雾太厚。可他算得出来：那炷香，这时候怕是只剩一截指头了。

他站在那里想了一想。他爹说过，堵在前头的东西，不一定要翻过去。他把身子一矮，趴在石阶上，从前头两个轿夫的腿缝里、从滑竿的杠子底下，像钻灌木丛撵獾子一样，一骨碌钻了过去。滑竿一晃。等马小宝回过头来找人，小满已经在五级之上了。马小宝却没有喊，他低头瞧着滑竿底下的石阶，瞧见了一样东西，伸手捞了起来，塞进了袖子里。小满回头瞧见了，没顾上多想。

最后那几十级，是在雾里走的。走着走着，雾一下子薄了。他抬起头来，只见雾在他脚底下，一整片的白，平平地铺开去，一直铺到天边，蒙山、泗水、县城、石坳村，统统给盖在了底下；雾上头，是明晃晃的太阳，是一层一层的殿宇，飞檐一角一角地翘起来，像一群正要起飞的鸟。他只看了一眼，便又低下头——最后一级到了。

最上头那一级，老头天没亮刚扫过，青石面上亮得能照见天。先上来的那几百个孩子，一个一个踩上去，踩出一片泥脚印，那老头便跟在后头，一下一下地扫。小满低头看了看自己的草鞋：走了三天的路，沾满了泥，前头还破了一个洞，一个脚趾头从洞里探出来。石坪上，守着铜炉的执事已经举起了手。小满抬起脚，又放下了，弯下腰，把草鞋底在上一级台阶的边沿上刮了刮，刮一下，看一看，又刮一下，刮干净了，这才抬脚，轻轻地踩了上去。扫地的老头正扫到他身边，扫帚停了一停。

执事的手落了下来：「香尽！」炉里最后一截香灰，恰在他那只脚落地的时候，断了。

执事走过来，伸手道：「考牌。」小满往怀里一摸——木牌还在，考牌没了。他把衣裳里里外外摸了三遍，摸出一身冷汗。执事等了一等，道：「牌子丢了，便算你没来过。」说着便要往下一个人那里走。

便在这时，那顶滑竿也上来了。小满想起滑竿底下，马小宝弯腰捞进袖子里的那样东西，道：「执事，我的考牌，在马少爷袖子里。」马小宝在滑竿上嚷道：「胡说！」扫地的老头正扫到滑竿边上，扫帚「笃」的一声，不轻不重，敲在滑竿的杠子上。滑竿一颤，马小宝的袖子一抖，一块竹牌「啪」地落在青石上。马小宝的脸红了又白，白了又青。执事捡起来，看了一眼上头烙的名字，递给小满，画了一道。扫地的老头一个字也没说，又低头扫地。

小满站在石坪边上，回过头去往下看了一眼。石阶一路垂下去，隐进白雾里，雾的底下，是几千个爹和娘，小得像地上的芝麻，哪一粒是舅舅，他一点也瞧不出来。一转头，那扫地的老头拄着扫帚，第一次抬起眼皮，正看着他——看他的脚，又看他的胸口，看他一起一伏的那口气。

小满心里「咯噔」一下。三百级走下来，他的气还是匀的——他洗过髓，又练了一年的吐纳，这老头看得出来么？他赶紧张大了嘴，呼哧呼哧地喘起粗气来，喘得像一只拉破了的风箱，舌头都吐出来半截，喘得跟方才那些坐在台阶上的孩子一模一样，一面喘，一面拿袖子擦汗，擦得十分卖力。扫地的老头看了他一会儿，道：「喘得好。」又扫地了。小满到底也没弄明白，这三个字，是夸他喘，还是夸他装。
story.en:
Shen Xiaoman didn't charge. He walked at the very back. His father had taught him: chasing rabbits you race for speed, chasing deer you race for steadiness; the road up a mountain belongs to the mountain, race the mountain and it won't let you by. Let them charge — the stair is three hundred steps; let them hurry — the incense is one stick: Xiaoman turned the two lines over and over in his head, walking step by step, three steps a breath in, three a breath out, looking only at the step under his feet.

The children charging out in front, round about the hundredth step, one after another seemed to have stones tied to their legs: some sat on the steps panting, mouths open, unable to straighten; some leaned on the cliff wall and shuffled step by step. Ma Xiaobao was carried up between two servants, one at each arm, his feet half a foot off the ground and swinging, still chewing osmanthus cake; the old sweeper glanced down from the top of the stair, the servants let go, and he dropped — *plop* — onto his backside on the hundred-and-twentieth step, slumped like a heap of wet mud. Xiaoman walked past him and didn't stop.

Around step one hundred and thirty he saw a boy from Yanzhou. The boy had charged up with the first wave, and now clung to the cliff wall, face white as paper, legs shaking like sieves. Seeing Xiaoman, his eyes lit as if at a rope thrown to a drowning man. "Brother! Pull me up!"

Xiaoman wanted to pull. But he knew that if he did, the breath of three steps in and three out would break; break the breath, and he'd be sitting down here himself. His father had said: when you meet someone fallen into a pit in the mountains, first see if your own feet are steady; if you're not steady yourself and reach out to pull, the two of you fall in together. So Xiaoman didn't reach out. He said only: "Stop charging. Three steps a breath. Follow my feet." The boy followed him a dozen steps, and at step one hundred and forty sat down after all, waving his hands. "Brother, you go, you go…" Xiaoman looked back at him once, and went. A dozen steps further up he heard the boy crying behind him, very quietly, as though afraid of being heard. He didn't look back; but he thought: the day I'm standing steady enough, I'll pull. As many as I can pull, I'll pull. The thought flashed and was gone; he didn't take it seriously then.

At the hundred-and-fiftieth step a girl with two little braids rushed past him. She didn't sit down and she didn't cry; all he saw was a profile with a nose frozen red, teeth gritted, charging up in one breath, braids flicking. Xiaoman's heart jumped: Ah He? A few days before he left she had stopped him at the well and asked how many days to the Si and how many flatbreads a day, and written it in a notebook he'd never seen — he'd thought she was asking for her father. He called, "Ah He!" The girl didn't look back; she charged straight up into the mist. A few steps higher, a dark, sturdy figure brushed past him too, head down, calloused at every knuckle — Shidan. He wasn't panting and he didn't look at anyone; every step came down hard, as if he meant to drive the stair into the mountain.

Step one hundred and sixty. It was no different from the other steps — only the cliff wall beside it had been carved, in who knew what years, with stones, with knives, with fingernails, crowded with writing, layer on layer: names, years, sometimes a single stroke — all carved by people who had sat down on this step. As he crossed it Xiaoman turned his head and looked once more among the carvings. He didn't know what he was looking for. He didn't find it.

Past one hundred and sixty the stair turned steep, each step half a finger higher than the one below, adding up by two hundred into a ladder; the cliff walls closed in, the narrow places only wide enough for two people sideways. He looked neither up nor down, only counted: one breath, two, three; lift the foot, set it down, lift again. From somewhere in the mist came a steady *shh, shh* — a broom on bluestone; with every step he climbed, it came a little nearer.

Around step two hundred and sixty there was a shout behind him: "Make way! Make way!" It was that sedan chair, coming up again. At the foot of the stair, it turned out, Ma San had brought out the letter; the steward glanced at the name it was signed with and said, "A letter. He may make it up." So the four bearers carried Ma Xiaobao up, jolting all the way, cake crumbs all over him. The chair squeezed past Xiaoman, pinning him to the cliff wall and scraping off a patch of skin. Having squeezed past, it stopped dead in the narrowest stretch ahead. Ma Xiaobao turned round in the chair and grinned at him. "Carry me slow. This young master's enjoying the view."

There was no view in the mist. The four bearers stood across the stair, front and back, blocking it so tight not a cat could get by. Xiaoman looked up — he couldn't see the burner; the mist was too thick. But he could reckon it: that stick of incense must be down to a finger's width by now.

He stood and thought a moment. His father had said: whatever blocks your way, you don't always have to go over it. He ducked low, dropped flat on the steps, and between the legs of the two front bearers, under the chair poles, the way you crawl through brush after a badger, rolled through. The chair lurched; Ma Xiaobao yelped, and his osmanthus cake dropped. By the time he turned round to look for him, Xiaoman was five steps above. Ma Xiaobao didn't shout, though. He was looking at the step under the chair; he'd seen something there. He reached down, scooped it up, and tucked it in his sleeve.

The last few dozen steps were climbed in mist. As he walked the mist suddenly thinned. He looked up: the mist lay under his feet, one sheet of white spread flat to the edge of the sky, Mount Meng, the Si, the county town, Shi'ao Village all covered beneath it; above it the blazing sun, and hall upon hall, the eaves tilting up corner after corner like a flock of birds about to take off. He looked just once, and lowered his head again — the last step had come.

The topmost step, swept by the old man before dawn, its bluestone bright enough to reflect the sky. The several hundred children who'd come up first had trodden on it one by one and left a sheet of muddy footprints, and the old man followed after them, sweeping stroke by stroke. Xiaoman looked down at his straw sandals: three days of road, caked in mud, a hole in the front with one toe poking out. On the terrace, the steward watching the burner had raised his hand. Xiaoman lifted his foot, then set it down again; bent over, scraped the sandal soles on the edge of the step below, scraped once, looked, scraped again, and when they were clean, lifted his foot and set it lightly on the step. The old sweeper, sweeping beside him just then, paused his broom.

The steward's hand came down: "The incense is out!" The last stub of ash in the burner broke just as that foot touched stone.

The steward came over and held out his hand. "Tag." Xiaoman felt inside his jacket — the wooden token was there; the trial tag was gone. He searched his clothes inside and out three times and came up with nothing but a cold sweat. The steward waited a moment. "Lose the tag and you were never here." And he turned to go to the next child.

Just then the sedan chair came up too. As it passed the old sweeper, the broom came down — *tok* — neither hard nor soft, on the chair's pole. The chair shook, Ma Xiaobao's sleeve shook, and something fell with a *clack* on the bluestone: a bamboo tally. Ma Xiaobao's face went red, then white, then green. The old sweeper bent, picked it up, glanced at the name branded on it, and without a word put it into Xiaoman's hand. Ma Xiaobao shouted from the chair: "I found it! I picked it up on the steps!" The old sweeper looked at him once. "Made it up." And bent to his sweeping again. The steward took Xiaoman's tag and drew one stroke on it.

Xiaoman stood at the edge of the terrace, and looked back down once. The stair hung down and vanished into white mist, and under the mist were several thousand fathers and mothers, small as sesame seeds; which seed was his uncle he couldn't tell at all. He turned round, and the old sweeper, leaning on his broom, had raised his eyelids for the first time and was looking at him — at his feet, then at his chest, at the breath rising and falling there.

Xiaoman's heart gave a jolt. Three hundred steps, and his breath was still even — he'd had his marrow washed, and a year of breathing practice; could this old man tell? He quickly opened his mouth wide and panted, huffing and puffing like a split bellows, tongue hanging half out, just like the children who'd been sitting on the steps, mopping sweat with his sleeve as he panted, very diligently. The old sweeper looked at him a while. "Well panted." And swept again. Xiaoman never did work out whether that meant the panting, or the pretending.

exits.means: rushes up the steps as fast as possible

story.zh:
小满也冲了。几千只鸭子里，多他一只不多。

冲到一百五十级上下，他的腿忽然沉了——不是累，是像有人往他两条腿上，一边挂了一块磨盘，越急，磨盘越重。身边的孩子一个接一个地坐下去，有的喘，有的哭。

走到一百五十级的时候，他从一个扎两根小辫子的姑娘身边走过去——不对，是那姑娘从他身边冲过去。她没坐下，也没哭，冲过他身边的时候，他只看见一个鼻头冻得通红的侧脸，像一根萝卜，咬着牙，一口气往上冲，冲得小辫子一甩一甩的。那个背影，瞧着有点眼熟。小满想多看两眼，她已经冲上去了，只剩一截小辫子在雾里一晃，就没了。

一百六十级。他停下来，扶着膝盖，大口大口地喘气。崖壁上刻满了字，都是在这一级上坐下过的人刻的。二十年前，舅舅在这儿坐了一炷香，看着别人一个一个从他身边走过去。

他想起他爹说的：追一头鹿，越急，鹿跑得越远。他站直了，三步一吸，三步一呼，不快，也不停。

香只剩一指的时候，他站在了第三百级石阶上，两条腿抖得像两根面条。扫地的老头抬起眼皮，看了他一眼，那一眼的意思大约是：鸭子里头，也有会自己停下来的。
story.en:
Xiaoman charged too. Among several thousand ducks, one more made no difference.

Around step one hundred and fifty his legs suddenly went heavy — not tired: as if someone had hung a millstone on each; the more he hurried, the heavier they got. Around him children sat down one after another, some panting, some crying.

At step one hundred and fifty he passed a girl with two little braids — no, it was she who passed him, charging. She didn't sit, didn't cry; charging past him, all he saw was a profile with a nose frozen red, like a radish, teeth gritted, charging up in one breath, braids flicking. That back looked a bit familiar. Xiaoman wanted a second look, but she'd already gone up; only the end of a braid flicked once in the mist, and was gone.

Step one hundred and sixty. He stopped, hands on his knees, gasping. The cliff wall was crowded with carvings — all by people who had sat down on this step. Twenty years ago his uncle had sat here the length of a stick of incense, watching others walk past him one by one.

He remembered his father's saying: chasing a deer, the more you hurry, the farther it runs. He straightened up — three steps in, three steps out; not fast, and not stopping.

With only a finger's width of incense left, he stood on the three hundredth step, legs shaking like two noodles. The old sweeper raised his eyelids and looked at him once; the look meant, roughly: even among ducks there's one that knows how to stop.
